body_md:
\label{thm1.3}
Let $N_{0}(X)$ be the number of integers $\leqslant X$ that are expressible as sums of two squares of integers. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be fixed. Uniformly for $X\geqslant 3$ and $X^{19/35+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X,$ one has
$$N_{0}(X+H)-N_{0}(X)=\frac{CH}{\log^{1/2} X}+O\left(\frac{H}{\log^{2/3-\varepsilon} X}\right), $$
where $C=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\prod_{p\equiv 3\,(\mathrm{mod}\,4)}(1-1/p^{2})^{-1/2}$ is the Landau--Ramanujan constant.

label: thm:intro-linear
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:intro-linear}
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and $X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon}$. Let $d,t\geqslant1$ be  integers and let $L\geqslant1$. Let $\Psi=(\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_t)$ be a system of affine linear forms $\psi_i\colon\mathbb Z^d\to\mathbb Z$ of the shape
$$
  \psi_i(\mathbf n)=\dot\psi_i\cdot \mathbf n+\psi_i(0),
  \qquad \dot\psi_i\in\mathbb Z^d,
$$
with $0<\|\dot\psi_i\|_\infty\leqslant L$ and $\left\lvert \psi_i(0)\right\rvert\leqslant LX$, and suppose that $\dot\psi_i$ and $\dot\psi_j$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ whenever $i\neq j$. Let $K\subset(X,X+H]^d$ be a convex body. Extend $\Lambda$ by zero to the nonpositive integers. Then,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-linear-theorem}
  \sum_{\mathbf n\in K\cap\mathbb Z^d}\prod_{i=1}^t\Lambda(\psi_i(\mathbf n))
  =\beta_\infty\prod_p\beta_p+o_{d,t,L,\varepsilon}(H^d),
\end{equation}
where
$$
  \beta_\infty=\operatorname{vol}\bigl(K\cap\Psi^{-1}(\mathbb R_{>0}^t)\bigr)
$$
and
$$
  \beta_p=\mathbb E_{\mathbf n\in(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^d}\prod_{i=1}^t \frac{p}{p-1}\1_{\psi_i(\mathbf n)\not\equiv0\pmod p}.
$$

name: Linear equations in primes in short intervals of exponent $3/5$

title: Remark
body_md:
Note that for all primes $p$ one has
$\beta_p=1+O_{d,t,L}(p^{-2})$. Thus the Euler product in
\eqref{eq:intro-linear-theorem} converges absolutely. It is zero if and only if
one of the local factors $\beta_p$ vanishes.

\label{def:function-K}
  We define the functions $\mathcal{K}, \mathcal{K}_0 \colon \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0} \times (0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ via
  \[
\mathcal{K}_0(\beta, \nu; \tau) := \min\left\{\tau+\beta(6\nu-2), \max\left\{\tau+\beta\left(4\nu-\frac{8}{5}\right), \frac{\tau}{2}+\beta(4\nu-1)\right\}, \tau+\beta(2\nu-1)\right\},
    \]
    and
    \[
      \mathcal{K}(\beta, \nu; \tau) := \min\left\{\tau, \max\left\{2\beta \nu, \mathcal{K}_0(\beta, \nu; \tau)\right\}\right\}.
      \]

head: environment
name: Large values estimates

label: eq:LVk=1
title: Proof
body_md:
\textbf{Proof of (i).} We first note that it suffices to prove
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:LVk=1}
    \mathcal{N}_A(\nu; [T, 2T])
    \ll X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta, \nu; \tau) +o(1)}.
  \end{equation}
  Indeed, let $k\in\mathbb N$ be fixed and write
  \[
    A(s)^k=\sum_{n\in \mathbb{N}}\frac{c_k(n)}{n^s}.
  \]
  The coefficients are supported on $N^k<n\leqslant2^kN^k$, where
  $N=X^\beta$, and satisfy
  \[
    |c_k(n)|\leqslant d_{Bk}(n) \log^{Bk} X.
  \]
  Split
  \[
    A(s)^k=\sum_{\ell=0}^{k-1}A_{k,\ell}(s),\qquad  A_{k,\ell}(s)=\sum_{2^\ell N^k<n\leqslant2^{\ell+1}N^k}\frac{c_k(n)}{n^s}.
  \]
  Let $\mathcal U\subseteq[T,2T]$ be a $1$-separated set on which
  \[
    |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta(1/2-\nu)}.
  \]
  Then, for every $t\in\mathcal U$, at least one
  $\ell\in\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$ satisfies
\[
|A_{k,\ell}(1/2+it)|\geqslant \frac1k X^{k\beta(1/2-\nu)}.
\]
  We partition $\mathcal U$ according to the least such $\ell$. Since
  $2^{\ell+1}N^k=X^{k\beta+O_k(1/\log X)}$, applying
  \eqref{eq:LVk=1} to each $A_{k,\ell}$, with the parameters changed
  by $O_{B,k,\beta,\nu}(1/\log X)$, gives
\[
    \#\mathcal U\ll_{B,k}X^{\mathcal K(k\beta,\nu;\tau)+o(1)},
\]
  where we used that $\mathcal K$ is piecewise linear. This proves the
  reduction to \eqref{eq:LVk=1}.

     We now turn to the proof of \eqref{eq:LVk=1}. Recall that $T = X^\tau$. If $\mathcal{K}(\beta, \nu; \tau) = \tau$, then $X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta, \nu; \tau)} = X^\tau = T$ and the claim is trivial. We may therefore assume henceforth that
      \begin{equation} \label{eq:Ksimp}
         \mathcal{K}(\beta, \nu; \tau) = \max\left\{2\beta \nu, \mathcal{K}_0(\beta, \nu; \tau)\right\} \leqslant \tau.
       \end{equation}
       
Set $N=X^\beta$ and $V=N^{1/2-\nu}$, and let
$\mathcal U\subseteq[T,2T]$ be any $1$-separated set such that
\[
  |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant V\qquad\text{for }t\in\mathcal U.
\]
Write
$$
  G\coloneqq \sum_{N<n\leqslant2N}\frac{|a(n)|^2}{n}\ll \log^{2B} X N^{-1}\sum_{N<n \leqslant 2N} d_B(n)^2\ll \log^{O_B(1)} X.
$$
By the second moment large values theorem \cite[Theorem~9.7]{IwaniecKowalski}, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:IK-thm-97-use}
  \#\mathcal{U}\ll (N+T)GV^{-2}\log(2N) \ll (X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau+\beta(2\nu-1)})X^{o(1)}.
\end{equation}
By Huxley's large values estimate in the form of \cite[Corollary~9.9]{IwaniecKowalski}, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:huxley-use}
  \#\mathcal{U}\ll \left(GNV^{-2}+G^3N TV^{-6}\right) \log^6 (2T) \ll (X^{2\beta \nu}+X^{\tau+\beta(6\nu-2)})X^{o(1)}.
\end{equation}

Next we apply the large value results of Guth and
Maynard~\cite{GuthMaynard}, together with the refinement due to Chen,
Gupta, and Li~\cite{CGCL}. Let $C_B$ be sufficiently large and set
\[
  A^\ast(it)\coloneqq N^{1/2-C_B/\log\log N}A(1/2+it)=\sum_{N<n\leqslant2N}b(n)n^{-it},
\]
where
\[
  b(n)=\frac{a(n)}{N^{C_B/\log\log N}}\left(\frac Nn\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The standard bound for the divisor function shows that if $C_B$ is large enough, then $|b(n)|\leqslant1$ for all $n$. Moreover, for
$t\in\mathcal U$,
\[
  |A^\ast(it)|\geqslant V^\ast,\qquad V^\ast\coloneqq N^{1-\nu-C_B/\log\log N}.
\]

Suppose first that $\beta\geqslant5\tau/6$. Then, for all sufficiently
large $X$,
\[
  N=X^\beta\geqslant(2T)^{2/3}.
\]
We may therefore apply
\cite[Theorem~1.1]{CGCL}, with $q=q_1=1$ and height $2T$, to the
points $-t$ with $t\in\mathcal U$. It gives
\[
  \#\mathcal U\ll (2T)^{o(1)}\left(N^2(V^\ast)^{-2}+(2T)^{1/2}N^3(V^\ast)^{-4}+2TN^2(V^\ast)^{-4}+2TN^{12/5}(V^\ast)^{-4}
  \right).
\]
The third term is dominated by the fourth. Since
$V^\ast=N^{1-\nu+o(1)}$, we obtain
\begin{equation} \label{eq:TboundGMbetasmall}
  \# \mathcal{U}\ll\left(X^{2\beta\nu}+X^{\tau/2+\beta(4\nu-1)}+X^{\tau+4\beta\nu-8\beta/5}\right)X^{o(1)}.
\end{equation}
If instead $\beta \leqslant 5\tau/6$, we have from \cite[Theorem 1.1]{GuthMaynard} with $V=N^{1-\nu+o(1)}$ that
\[
\# \mathcal U\ll \big(X^{2\beta \nu}+ X^{\tau +\beta(4\nu-8/5)} + X^{\beta(4\nu-2/5)}\big) X^{o(1)}.
\]
Noting that $\beta (4\nu-2/5) \leqslant \tau/2 +4\beta \nu -\beta$ whenever $\beta \leqslant 5\tau/6$, we can also conclude estimate~\eqref{eq:TboundGMbetasmall} in this case.
 
Now~\eqref{eq:LVk=1} follows by comparing the estimates~\eqref{eq:IK-thm-97-use},~\eqref{eq:huxley-use}, and~\eqref{eq:TboundGMbetasmall} with~\eqref{eq:Ksimp} and the definition of $\mathcal{K}_0(\beta, \nu; \tau)$. 

\textbf{Proof of~(ii).} Now we assume that $a(n) = \mathbf{1}_{n \in I} \chi(n) \log^r n$ for some Dirichlet character $\chi$ of modulus $\ll \log^{O(1)} X$, some interval $I \subseteq (X^\beta, 2X^\beta]$, and some $r \in \{0, 1\}$.

Write $N=X^\beta$. Perron's formula and the fourth moment estimate for Dirichlet $L$-functions give that there is a constant
$C_0=C_0(B)>0$ such that, for every $1$-separated set
$\mathcal U\subseteq[T,2T]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourth-moment-sublemma}
 \sum_{t\in\mathcal U}|A(1/2+it)|^4
 \ll \left(T+\#\mathcal U\left(\frac{1}{T^2}+\frac{N^2}{T^4}\right)
 \right)\log^{C_0} X;
\end{equation}
this follows from the proof of
\cite[Lemma~9]{BakerHarmanPintz1997} and partial summation to remove
the coefficients $\log^r n$.

Let $\nu\geqslant0$ be arbitrary. Let $\mathcal U$ be a $1$-separated subset of
\[
 \left\{t\in\mathcal T:
 |A(1/2+it)|\geqslant N^{1/2-\nu}\right\}.
\]
We choose the constant $C=C(B)$ in \eqref{eq:4thmomcond} so that
$4C>C_0+10$. If $\nu\geqslant1/2$, the trivial bound
$\#\mathcal U\ll T$ for a $1$-separated subset of $[T,2T]$ gives
\[
 \mathcal N_A(\nu;\mathcal T)
 \ll T
 \leqslant X^{\tau+2\beta(2\nu-1)},
\]
so we may suppose that $\nu<1/2$.

The definition of $\mathcal U$ and
\eqref{eq:fourth-moment-sublemma} give
\begin{align}
 \#\mathcal U
 &\ll
 N^{4\nu-2}T\log^{C_0} X +
 \#\mathcal U
 \left(
 N^{4\nu-2}T^{-2}+N^{4\nu}T^{-4}
 \right)\log^{C_0} X.
 \label{eq:fourth-moment-absorption}
\end{align}
Since $\nu<1/2$ and $\tau > 1/\sqrt{\log X}$, we have
\begin{equation} \label{eq:fthtriv}
 N^{4\nu-2}T^{-2}\log^{C_0} X=o(1).
\end{equation}

Now, let $\nu_1$ be defined by
\[
 N^{1/2-\nu_1}=\frac{N^{1/2}}{T}\log^C X.
\]
The hypothesis $\tau>1/\sqrt{\log X}$ gives, for all sufficiently
large $X$,
\[
 \nu_1
 =\frac{\tau\log X-C\log\log X}{\beta\log X}
 >0.
\]
If $\nu_1\leqslant\nu$, assumption~\eqref{eq:4thmomcond} shows that every
$t\in\mathcal T$ belongs to the level sets corresponding to both
$\nu_1$ and $\nu$. Hence
\[
 \mathcal N_A(\nu;\mathcal T)
 =
 \mathcal N_A(\nu_1;\mathcal T),
\]
and it is enough to prove~\eqref{eq:fourthMomentN} with $\nu_1$ in
place of $\nu$. We may therefore replace $\nu$ by $\nu_1$ in this
case and hence assume that $\nu\leqslant\nu_1$. It follows that
\[
 N^{4\nu}T^{-4}\leqslant N^{4\nu_1}T^{-4}= \frac{1}{\log^{4C} X}.
\]
Combining with~\eqref{eq:fourth-moment-absorption} and~\eqref{eq:fthtriv} we obtain
\[
 \#\mathcal U
 \ll
 N^{4\nu-2}T\log^{C_0} X + o(\#\mathcal U)
 =
 X^{\tau+2\beta(2\nu-1)+o(1)} + o(\#\mathcal U),
\]
and~\eqref{eq:fourthMomentN} follows. This completes the proof of the lemma.

name: Sparse mean square

label: eq:sparse-mean-square-discrete2
title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is a slight variant of the proof of the Hal\'asz--Montgomery mean value theorem (see e.g.~\cite[Theorem 9.6]{IwaniecKowalski}). For a similar variant for prime-supported Dirichlet polynomials, see~\cite[Lemma 4.4]{MRII}.

  By the duality principle (see e.g.~\cite[Section 7.1]{IwaniecKowalski}), it suffices to show that, for any complex coefficients $c(t)$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sparse-mean-square-discrete2}
\sum_{N < n \leqslant 2N}\left| \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t) n^{-it}\right|^2 \ll \left(N+|\mathcal{U}| T^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}} N^{1-\eta}\log^{2/3} T\right) \sum_{t \in \mathcal{U}} |c(t)|^2.
\end{equation}
Let $w$ be a smooth non-negative compactly supported function such that $w(x) = 1$ for $x \in [1,2]$. Its Mellin transform
\[
  \widetilde{w}(z)=\int_0^\infty w(x)x^{z-1}\,\textnormal{d} x
\]
satisfies, for $1/2\leqslant\sigma\leqslant2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mellin-decay-sparse}
  \widetilde w(\sigma+it)\ll(1+|t|)^{-10}.
\end{equation}

By inserting this smooth weight $w$, we have
\begin{align} \label{eq:HM1ststep}
\sum_{N < n \leqslant 2N}\left| \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t) n^{-it}\right|^2 \leqslant \sum_{n} w\left(\frac{n}{N} \right)\left| \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t) n^{-it}\right|^2 = \sum_{t_1, t_2 \in \mathcal{U}} c(t_1)\overline{c(t_2)} \sum_{n} w\left(\frac{n}{N} \right) n^{-i(t_1-t_2)}.
\end{align}
For the inner summation, Mellin inversion on a line $c>1$ gives
\[
w\left(\frac{n}{N} \right) =\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty} \widetilde w (z) N^zn^{-z} \,\textnormal{d} z.
\]
Hence
\[
  \sum_{n} w\left(\frac{n}{N} \right) n^{-i(t_1-t_2)} =\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\widetilde w(z)N^z\zeta(z+i(t_1-t_2))\,\textnormal{d} z.
\]
Moving the contour to $\operatorname{Re}(z)=1-\eta$ crosses a pole at $z=1+i(t_2-t_1)$. This gives
\[
 \sum_{n} w\left(\frac{n}{N} \right) n^{-i(t_1-t_2)} = \widetilde w(1+i (t_2-t_1)) N^{1+ i(t_2-t_1)} +\frac{1}{2\pi i} \int_{1-\eta-i\infty}^{1-\eta+i\infty} \widetilde w(z)N^z\zeta(z+i(t_1-t_2))\,\textnormal{d} z.
\]
We bound the integral using \eqref{eq:mellin-decay-sparse} and a result of Ford~\cite[Theorem 1]{Ford02}, which for $|t|\geqslant3$ and $\sigma \in [1/2, 1]$ gives
\[
  |\zeta(\sigma+it)| \leqslant 100 (|t|+1)^{\frac{9}{2}(1-\sigma)^{3/2}} \log^{2/3} (|t|+2).
  \]
For $|t|\leqslant3$, we instead use
$|\zeta(1-\eta+it)|\ll_\eta 1$. This leads to
\begin{align*}
 &\left|
 \int_{1-\eta-i\infty}^{1-\eta+i\infty}
 \widetilde w(z)N^z\zeta(z+i(t_1-t_2))\,\textnormal{d} z
 \right|\\
 &\leqslant N^{1-\eta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
 |\widetilde w(1-\eta+iu)|
 |\zeta(1-\eta+i(u+t_1-t_2))|\,\,\textnormal{d} u\\
 &\ll_\eta N^{1-\eta}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
 \frac{(|u+t_1-t_2|+1)^{\frac92\eta^{3/2}}
 \log^{2/3}(|u+t_1-t_2|+2)}
 {(1+|u|)^{10}}\,\,\textnormal{d} u\\
 &\ll_\eta N^{1-\eta}
 (1+|t_1|+|t_2|)^{\frac92\eta^{3/2}}
 \log^{2/3}(2+|t_1|+|t_2|).
\end{align*}
Thus, one concludes from~\eqref{eq:HM1ststep} and the above estimates that
\begin{align*}
\sum_{N < n \leqslant 2N}\left| \sum_{t\in\mathcal{U}}c(t) n^{-it}\right|^2 &\ll N \sum_{t_1,t_2\in \mathcal U} |c(t_1) \overline{c(t_2)}| \cdot|\widetilde w(1+i (t_2-t_1))| \\
&+ N^{1-\eta} \sum_{t_1,t_2\in \mathcal U} |c(t_1)\overline{c(t_2)}| (1+|t_1|+|t_2|)^{\frac{9}{2}\eta^{3/2}} \log^{2/3}(2+|t_1|+|t_2|).
\end{align*}
The claim~\eqref{eq:sparse-mean-square-discrete2} now follows from the inequality $|c(t_1)\overline{c(t_2)}| \leqslant (|c(t_1)|^2+|c(t_2)|^2)/2$, the rapid decay of $\widetilde{w}$ (see~\eqref{eq:mellin-decay-sparse}) and the assumption that $\mathcal{U}$ is $1$-separated.

We argue by contradiction and assume that~\eqref{eq:minHjbound} fails. Thus there exist $y_1, \dotsc, y_J \in I$ and $t_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that

     \min_{j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}} H_j(y_j) \geqslant t_0 \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^J \beta_j y_j -\varepsilon_0.

    By the range of $H_j$, we can assume that $t_0 \in [0, \tau].$ For each $j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$, by the definition of $P_j(t)$, the inequality $H_j(y_j) \geqslant t_0$ implies that $P_j(t_0) \leqslant \beta_j y_j$. Thus

     t_0 \geqslant \sum_{j = 1}^J \beta_j y_j -\varepsilon_0 \geqslant \sum_{j=1}^J P_j(t_0) - \varepsilon_0.

    Consequently, the assumption~\eqref{eq:SumPjbound} fails, and the claim follows.

body_md:
\label{prop:one-var-check} 
  Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small but fixed and let $B \geqslant 1$. Let $X \geqslant 2,\, T = X^\tau$ with $\tau \in (0, 1/2)$ and let $\mathcal{T} \subseteq [T, 2T]$. Let $J \geqslant 3$ be a fixed integer and let $\beta_j \geqslant \varepsilon$ for $j = 1, \dotsc, J$ be numbers satisfying $\beta_1 + \dotsb + \beta_J = 1$. For $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$, let
$$
  A_j(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta_j} <n\leqslant2X^{\beta_j}} a_{j}(n) n^{-s},
$$
be a Dirichlet polynomial for which $a_j(n) \ll d_B(n) \log^B X$ for all $n$. Suppose that there exists $j_0 \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$ such that
  \[
   \sup_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \big|A_{j_0}(1/2+it) \big| \ll_C \frac{X^{\beta_{j_0}/2}}{\log^C X}
    \]
for every $C \geqslant 1.$

For each $1\leqslant j\leqslant J$, suppose that the function $H_j\colon\mathbb R_{\geqslant0}\to[0,\tau]$ is such that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:NAjbound}
  \mathcal N_{A_j}(\nu;\mathcal T)
  \leqslant X^{H_j(\nu)+\varepsilon^{20}}
\end{equation}
for all $\nu\in[\varepsilon^6,\varepsilon^{-1}]$.
Define the functions $P_j\colon[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty]$ via
\[
P_{j}(t) = \inf\{\beta_j \nu \colon \nu \in [\varepsilon^6, \varepsilon^{-1}], H_j(\nu) \geqslant t\}.
\]
Assume that
\[
\sum_{j = 1}^J P_j(t) > t+\varepsilon^{10} \qquad\text{ for every } t \in [0, \tau].
 \]
Then
\begin{equation*}
\int_{\mathcal{T}} |A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it) \dotsm A_J(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d} t\ll_{\varepsilon, A, B} \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}
\end{equation*}
for every $A>0$.

label: eq:Sdef
title: Proof
body_md:
By a standard reduction, it suffices to show that, for any $1$-separated subset $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ we have, for any $A \geqslant 1$,
\begin{align}\label{eq:Sdef}
   \sum_{t\in\mathcal U}
  |A_1(1/2+it)\dotsm A_J(1/2+it)| \ll_{\varepsilon, A, B} \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X} 
\end{align}
  We split $\mathcal{U} = \mathcal{U}_1 \sqcup \mathcal{U}_2 \sqcup \mathcal{U}_3$, where $\mathcal{U}_1$ consists of those $t \in \mathcal{U}$ for which there exists $j_1 \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$ such that $|A_{j_1}(1/2+it)| \leqslant X^{-1/2}$, $\mathcal{U}_2$ consists of those $t \in \mathcal{U} \setminus \mathcal{U}_1$ for which there exists $j_2 \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$ such that $|A_{j_2}(1/2+it)| \geqslant X^{\beta_{j_2}(1/2-\varepsilon^6)}$, and finally, we set $\mathcal{U}_3 = \mathcal{U} \setminus (\mathcal{U}_1 \cup \mathcal{U}_2)$. It suffices to show that, for each $k \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, we have
  \[
    S_k := \sum_{t \in \mathcal{U}_k} |A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it) \dotsm A_J(1/2+it)| \ll_{\varepsilon, A, B} \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X} 
    \]
    for every $A \geqslant 1$.

    \textbf{Estimation of $S_1.$} For $j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$, let $\mathcal U_{1,j}$ consist of those $t\in\mathcal U_1$ for which $j$ is the least index satisfying
\[
  |A_j(1/2+it)|\leqslant X^{-1/2}.
\]
Then $\mathcal U_1=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^J\mathcal U_{1,j}$.
For $t \in \mathcal{U}_{1, j}$ we use for $\ell \neq j$ the crude estimate
    \[
    |A_\ell(1/2+it)| \leqslant \sum_{X^{\beta_\ell}< n \leqslant 2X^{\beta_\ell}} \frac{|a_\ell(n)|}{n^{1/2}} \ll X^{\beta_\ell/2+o(1)}.
    \]
    Combining this estimate with the fact that $\beta_1+\cdots+\beta_J=1$ and $\beta_j\geqslant \varepsilon$, we then deduce that the contribution of $\mathcal{U}_{1, j}$ to $S_1$ is
  \[
\#\mathcal{U}_{1, j} \cdot \frac{1}{X^{1/2}} \cdot X^{(1-\beta_{j})/2+o(1)} \leqslant \#\mathcal{U}_{1, j} \cdot X^{-\varepsilon/2+o(1)}.
    \]
Since $\#\mathcal{U} \ll X^\tau \leqslant X^{1/2}$, we obtain, for all sufficiently large $X$ and any $A \geqslant 1$, that
\[
  S_1\ll \#\mathcal{U}_{1} \cdot X^{-\varepsilon/2+o(1)} \ll_{\varepsilon, A} \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}.
\]
    
    \textbf{Estimation of $S_2$.} Let us first bound $\# \mathcal{U}_{2}$. For $j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$, let $\mathcal U_{2,j}$ consist of those $t\in\mathcal U_2$ for which $j$ is the least index satisfying
\[
  |A_j(1/2+it)|\geqslant X^{\beta_j(1/2-\varepsilon^6)}.
\]
Then $\mathcal U_2=\bigsqcup_{j=1}^J\mathcal U_{2,j}$. Let $j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$. Choose $k_j\in\mathbb N$ so that $k_j\beta_j\in[1,2]$. Lemma~\ref{le:MVHuGM}, applied to $\mathcal U_{2,j}$ with $k=k_j$ and $\nu=\varepsilon^6$, gives
\[
  \#\mathcal U_{2,j}
  \ll X^{\min\{\tau,\max\{2k_j\beta_j\varepsilon^6,
       \mathcal K_0(k_j\beta_j,\varepsilon^6;\tau)\}\}+o(1)}.
\]
Since
\[
\mathcal K_0(k_j\beta_j,\varepsilon^6;\tau)\leqslant \tau+k_j\beta_j(2\varepsilon^6-1)\leqslant \tau+2\varepsilon^6-1<0,
\]
we obtain
\[
\#\mathcal U_2 \ll \sum_{j=1}^J X^{2k_j\beta_j\varepsilon^6+o(1)}\ll_\varepsilon X^{4\varepsilon^6+o(1)}.
\]

To estimate $S_2$, we next partition $\{1,\dotsc,J\}=\{j_0\}\sqcup\mathcal J_1\sqcup\mathcal J_2$, where $\mathcal J_1$ and $\mathcal J_2$ are non-empty, and, for $k\in\{1,2\}$, set
\[
  M_k=\prod_{j\in\mathcal J_k}X^{\beta_j},\qquad
  B_k(s)=\prod_{j\in\mathcal J_k}A_j(s)
       =\sum_{M_k<n\leqslant2^{|\mathcal J_k|}M_k}\frac{b_k(n)}{n^s}.
\]
Splitting each $B_k(s)$ into $O_\varepsilon(1)$ dyadic Dirichlet polynomials and applying Lemma~\ref{lem:sparse-mean-square} with $\eta=\varepsilon^4$ to each of them, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
  \sum_{t\in\mathcal U_2}|B_k(1/2+it)|^2
  &\ll\left(M_k+|\mathcal U_2|T^{\frac92\varepsilon^6}
       M_k^{1-\varepsilon^4}\right)\log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)} X\\
  &\ll M_k\left(1+X^{10\varepsilon^6-\varepsilon^5}\right)
       \log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)} X
  \ll M_k\log^{O_{B,\varepsilon}(1)} X
\end{align*}
once $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small. Thus, by the pointwise bound for $A_{j_0}(1/2+it)$ and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, we obtain, for any $C \geqslant 1$,
      \[
        S_2 \ll_{B, C} \frac{X^{\beta_{j_0}/2}}{\log^C X} (M_1M_2)^{1/2} \log^{O(1)} X.
       \]
This is $\ll X^{1/2}/\log^A X$ for any $A \geqslant 1$.

\textbf{Estimation of $S_3$.} We split into level sets according to the sizes of $|A_j(1/2+it)|$.

For $j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}$, we define
\[
  \nu_{j,\ell}=\min\left\{
    \varepsilon^{-1},\varepsilon^6+\frac{\ell\log2}{\beta_j\log X}\right\},\qquad 0\leqslant\ell\leqslant L_j
\]
with
\[
  L_j=\left\lceil\frac{\beta_j(\varepsilon^{-1}-\varepsilon^6)\log X}{\log2}\right\rceil.
\]

Now
\[
\beta_j\left(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j, 0}\right) = \beta_j\left(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon^6\right), \quad \beta_j\left(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j, L_j}\right) \leqslant \beta_j\left(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon^{-1}\right) \leqslant -\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Thus, for every $t\in\mathcal U_3$ and every $j$, there is an
$\ell_j\in\{0,\ldots,L_j-1\}$ such that
\[
 X^{\beta_j(1/2-\nu_{j,\ell_j+1})}<|A_j(1/2+it)|\leqslant X^{\beta_j(1/2-\nu_{j,\ell_j})}.
\]

Partitioning $\mathcal U_3$ according to
$(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_J)$, and using
\[
  0\leqslant \beta_j(\nu_{j,\ell_j+1}-\nu_{j,\ell_j})\leqslant\frac{\log2}{\log X},
\]
we obtain
\[
 S_3\ll 2^J \log^J X \max_{\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_J}X^{\sum_{j=1}^J\beta_j(\frac{1}{2}-\nu_{j,\ell_j+1})}\min_j \mathcal{N}_{A_j}(\nu_{j, \ell_j+1}; \mathcal{U}_3).
\]
In particular by assumption~\eqref{eq:NAjbound}, we have $S_3 \ll X^{1/2} \log^{-A} X$ if
\[
\min_{j \in \{1, \dotsc, J\}} H_j(\nu_j) \leqslant \beta_1 \nu_1 +\dotsb + \beta_J \nu_J- \varepsilon^{10} \quad \text{for every $\nu_1, \dotsc, \nu_J \in [\varepsilon^6,\varepsilon^{-1}]$}.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{le:inversecost}, this happens if, for every $t \in [0, \tau]$, we have
\[
\sum_{j = 1}^J P_j(t) > t + \varepsilon^{10},
\]
    and the claim follows.

body_md:
\label{lem:hbi-trilinear-estimates}
  Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $B \geqslant 1$. Set $T_0\coloneqq \exp(\log^{1/4} X)$ and let
$$
T_1=X^{\tau_1},\qquad \tau_1 := \frac{16}{35}-\varepsilon.
$$
Let $\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3 \in [\varepsilon, \tau_1]$ be such that $\beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 = 1$. For $j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, let
$$
A_j(s)=\sum_{X^{\beta_j} <n\leqslant2X^{\beta_j}} a_{j}(n) n^{-s},
$$
where $|a_j(n)|\ll d_B(n)\log^B X$. Assume further that
$a_1(n)=\mathbf1_{n\in I}\chi(n)\log^r n$ for some interval
$I\subseteq(X^{\beta_1},2X^{\beta_1}]$, some $r\in\{0,1\}$,
and some Dirichlet character $\chi$ of modulus $\ll\log^B X$.

Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:hbi-trilinear-integral}
  \int_{T_0}^{T_1} |A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it)A_3(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d} t \ll_{A, B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}
\end{equation}
for every $A>0$.

name: Heath-Brown--Iwaniec trilinear estimates

label: le:16/35comput
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Notice first that by our assumption on the coefficients $a_1(n)$ (use e.g.~\cite[Lemma~3.9(i)]{MSTT} and partial summation), we have for every $A > 0$ the bound
\[
\sup_{T_0 \leqslant t \leqslant T_1} |A_1(1/2+it)| \ll \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{\log^A X}.
\]
Combining the preceding bound with the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and the mean value theorem gives, for every $A > 0$,
  \begin{align*}
    &\int_{T_0}^{X^\varepsilon} |A_1(1/2+it) A_2(1/2+it) A_3(1/2+it)| \,\textnormal{d} t \\
    &\ll_A \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{\log^A X} \left(\int_{T_0}^{X^\varepsilon} |A_2(1/2+it)|^2 \,\textnormal{d} t \int_{T_0}^{X^\varepsilon} |A_3(1/2+it)|^2 \,\textnormal{d} t\right)^{1/2} \\
    &\ll_{A, B} \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{\log^A X} \left((X^\varepsilon+X^{\beta_2})(X^\varepsilon+X^{\beta_3})\right)^{1/2} \log^{O_B(1)} X.
  \end{align*}
Since $\beta_2, \beta_3 \geqslant \varepsilon$ and $\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3=1$, the right-hand side is $\ll X^{1/2}/\log^A X$ for every $A > 0$.
  
Thus, by dyadic splitting, it suffices to show that, for every
$T\in[X^\varepsilon,T_1]$ and
\[
\mathcal I_T=[T,\min\{2T,T_1\}],
\]
we have
\[
\int_{\mathcal I_T} |A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it)A_3(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d} t\ll_{A, B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}.
  \]
Let $C = C(B)$ be as in Lemma~\ref{le:MVHuGM}(ii) and let
$\mathcal I_T=\mathcal{T}_1\sqcup\mathcal{T}_2$, where
$\mathcal{T}_1$ consists of those $t\in\mathcal I_T$ for which
  \[
    |A_1(1/2+it)| < \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{T} \log^C X
    \]
and $\mathcal{T}_2=\mathcal I_T\setminus\mathcal{T}_1$.

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and the mean value theorem (see e.g.~\cite[Theorem 9.1]{IwaniecKowalski}) it follows that
\begin{align*}
    &\int_{\mathcal{T}_1} |A_1(1/2+it) A_2(1/2+it) A_3(1/2+it)| \,\textnormal{d} t \\
    &\ll \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{T} \log^C X \left(\int_{\mathcal{T}_1} |A_2(1/2+it)|^2 \,\textnormal{d} t \int_{\mathcal{T}_1} |A_3(1/2+it)|^2 \,\textnormal{d} t\right)^{1/2} \\
    &\ll_B \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{T} \left((T+X^{\beta_2})(T+X^{\beta_3})\right)^{1/2} \log^{O_B(1)} X \\
    &\ll_B \left(X^{\beta_1/2} + \frac{X^{(\beta_1+\beta_2)/2}+X^{(\beta_1+\beta_3)/2}}{T_0^{1/2}} + \frac{X^{(\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3)/2}}{T_0}\right) \log^{O_B(1)} X \\
  &\ll_{A, B} \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}
  \end{align*}
  for every $A > 0$.
  
  Thus it suffices to show that
  \[
   \int_{\mathcal{T}_2} |A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it)A_3(1/2+it)|\,\textnormal{d} t \ll_{A,B}\frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X}.
  \]
Write $T=X^\tau$ with $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\tau_1]$. Note that, for
$t\in\mathcal T_2$, one has
\[
  |A_1(1/2+it)|
  \geqslant \frac{X^{\beta_1/2}}{T}\log^C X.
\]
We deduce from Lemma~\ref{le:MVHuGM}(i) and (ii) that, for every
$\nu\geqslant0$,
\[
  \mathcal N_{A_1}(\nu;\mathcal T_2)
  \ll
  X^{\max\left\{0,
  \min\{\tau+2\beta_1(2\nu-1),
  \mathcal K(2\beta_1,\nu;\tau)\}\right\}+o(1)}.
\]
Besides, for $j \in \{2, 3\}$ and $\nu\geqslant0$, we have by Lemma~\ref{le:MVHuGM}
\[
  \mathcal N_{A_j}(\nu ; \mathcal{T}_2)\ll \min\{X^{\mathcal{K}(\beta_j,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}, X^{\mathcal{K}(2\beta_j,\nu;\tau)+o(1)}\}.
  \]
The desired estimate now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:one-var-check} and Lemma~\ref{le:16/35comput}. This completes the proof.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem4.3}
The example $(\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3)=(1/5,2/5,2/5)$ is a limiting case which shows that one cannot take $\tau_{1} = 16/35$ in Lemma~\ref{le:16/35comput}: Set $\nu=2/7$ and observe that then
$$H_{1,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+2\beta_{1}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{6\beta_{1}}{7}=2/7,$$
$$H_{2,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+\beta_{2}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{3\beta_{2}}{7}=2/7,$$ 
$$H_{3,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)=\tau_{1}+\beta_{3}(2\nu-1)=\tau_{1}-\frac{3\beta_{3}}{7}=2/7.$$
Hence, taking $t=2/7$ it follows that $P_{j,\tau_{1}}(2/7)\leqslant 2\beta_{j}/7$ for each $1\leqslant j\leqslant 3$, and thus
$$P_{1,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)+P_{2,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)+P_{3,\tau_{1}}\Big(\frac{2}{7}\Big)\leqslant \frac{2}{7}=t,$$ so~\eqref{eq:HBICompPjClaim} does not hold.

In more classical language, these computations correspond to the fact that with current understanding of the large values of Dirichlet polynomials, we cannot rule out the scenario that
\begin{align*}
 \left|\sum_{n\sim X^{\beta_j}} \frac{a_j(n)}{n^{1/2+it}}\right|\geqslant X^{\beta_j(1/2-2/7)}\qquad j=1,2,3
\end{align*}
for $\gg X^{2/7}$ one-separated points $t\in[-X^{\tau_1},X^{\tau_1}]$, where $a_1(n)=1$ and $|a_j(n)|\ll d_B(n)$ for $j=2,3$ and some fixed $B$. 

In order to obtain the exponent $19/35-\varepsilon$ in Theorems \ref{thm:intro-mobius}, \ref{thm1.3}, \ref{thm1.4} and \ref{thm1.5}, we would need to essentially have the bound
\[
\int_{X^\varepsilon}^{X^{\tau_1+\varepsilon}}  \left|\sum_{n \sim X^{1/5}} \frac{1}{n^{1/2+it}}\right|^5 \,\textnormal{d} t \ll \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X},
\]
and it is the above-mentioned scenario which prevents us from obtaining this.

label: lem:gowers-gluing
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Gluing Gowers norms on adjacent intervals

title: Proof
body_md:
Set
\[
  m=\left\lceil\frac{H}{L}\right\rceil,\qquad \ell=\frac{H}{m}.
\]
Then $L/2<\ell\leqslant L$. Partition $I$ into the consecutive intervals
\[
  I_j=(a+j\ell,a+(j+1)\ell],\qquad 0\leqslant j<m,
\]
and write $f_j=f\1_{I_j}$.

For a tuple $\boldsymbol{i}=(i_\omega)_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^s}$, with each $i_\omega\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$, set
\[
  \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}} =\sum_{x,h_1,\ldots,h_s\in\mathbb Z} \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^s}\mathcal C^{|\omega|}f_{i_\omega}(x+\omega_1h_1+\cdots+\omega_sh_s).
\]
By multilinearity, we have
\begin{equation} \label{eq:f1InormLambdai}
  \|f\1_I\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}^{2^s}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{i}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}.
\end{equation}

We first count the tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ for which
$\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}$ can be nonzero. Suppose that such a tuple $\boldsymbol{i}$ is fixed and let $x,h_1,\ldots, h_s$ be such that $\prod_{\omega\in \{0,1\}^s}\mathcal{C}^{|\omega|}f_{i_{\omega}}(x+\omega_1h_1+\cdots+\omega_sh_s)\neq 0$. Writing, for $\omega \in \{0, 1\}^s$,
\[
  n_\omega=x+\omega_1h_1+\cdots+\omega_sh_s,
\]
we have
\[
  n_\omega=(1-|\omega|)n_{\boldsymbol{0}}+\sum_{r=1}^s\omega_r n_{\boldsymbol{e}_r}.
\]
The condition $n_\omega\in I_{i_\omega}$ gives
\[
  i_\omega=(1-|\omega|)i_{\boldsymbol{0}}+\sum_{r=1}^s\omega_r i_{\boldsymbol{e}_r}+O_s(1).
\]
Therefore, once
\[
  i_{\boldsymbol{0}},i_{\boldsymbol{e}_1},\ldots,i_{\boldsymbol{e}_s}
\]
have been chosen, there are only $O_s(1)$ possibilities for every
remaining $i_\omega$. Hence at most $O_s(m^{s+1})$
tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ contribute.

For each such tuple, the Gowers--Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
\begin{equation} \label{eq:afterGCS}
  |\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}|\leqslant \prod_{\omega\in\{0,1\}^s} \|f_{i_\omega}\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}.
\end{equation}

Writing
\begin{equation*}
  \eta=
  \max_{\substack{I'\subseteq I\text{ an interval}\\ L/2<|I'|\leqslant L}}
  \|f\|_{U^s(I')},
\end{equation*}
we have
\[
  \|f_j\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}\leqslant \eta\|\1_{I_j}\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}\ll_s \eta\ell^{(s+1)/2^s}.
\]
Combining this with~\eqref{eq:afterGCS} yields
\[
  |\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{i}}|\ll_s \eta^{2^s}\ell^{s+1}.
\]
Summing over the $O_s(m^{s+1})$ possible tuples $\boldsymbol{i}$ that contribute non-trivially to~\eqref{eq:f1InormLambdai}, we obtain
\begin{equation} \label{eq:F1Iest}
  \|f\1_I\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}^{2^s}\ll_s\eta^{2^s}m^{s+1}\ell^{s+1}=\eta^{2^s}H^{s+1}.
\end{equation}
Finally,
\begin{equation} \label{eq:1Iest}
  \|\1_I\|_{U^s(\mathbb Z)}^{2^s}\asymp_s H^{s+1}.
\end{equation}
Dividing~\eqref{eq:F1Iest} by~\eqref{eq:1Iest} and taking $2^s$-th roots proves the claim.

label: lem:comb3/5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:comb3/5}
Let $k\geqslant 1$ and let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\geqslant0$ with $\sum_{j\leqslant k}\alpha_j=1$. For $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$ write $\alpha_J=\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_j$. At least one of the following alternatives holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $\alpha_j\geqslant2/5$ for some $j$.
\item $\alpha_j+\alpha_\ell\geqslant3/5$ for some distinct $j,\ell$.
\item There is a subset $J^*$ with $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J^*}\leqslant3/5$, and there is a partition $\{1,\ldots,k\}=J_1\sqcup J_2\sqcup J_3$ such that $\alpha_{J_r}\in [1/10, 1/2]$ for $r=1,2,3$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Type I, Type $\mathrm{I}_2$, Type II trichotomy

title: Proof
body_md:
We assume that both \emph{(i)} and \emph{(ii)} fail and will show that case \emph{(iii)} must hold. We begin by finding a set $J^*$ such that $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J^*}\leqslant3/5$. Without loss of generality, suppose $\alpha_1\geqslant \alpha_2\geqslant \cdots \geqslant\alpha_k\geqslant 0$.

  If $\alpha_2\geqslant 1/5$, then we set $J^* =\{1,2\}$ and the desired bound follows from $\alpha_1\geqslant \alpha_2$ and the assumption that $\alpha_1+\alpha_2<3/5$.

  Otherwise, let $j^*$ be the least index such that $\sum_{1\leqslant j\leqslant j^*} \alpha_j\geqslant 2/5$ and set $J^*=\{1,2,\dots,j^*\}$. Since we are not in case \emph{(i)}, we have $j^*\geqslant 2$, and hence $\alpha_{j^*} \leqslant \alpha_2 < 1/5$. Therefore,
\[
\frac{2}{5} \leqslant \alpha_{J^*} = \sum_{1\leqslant j<j^*} \alpha_j+ \alpha_{j^*} < \frac{2}{5} + \frac{1}{5} = \frac{3}{5}.
\]
Therefore, such a set $J^*$ exists in both cases.

Set $J_1=J^*$ if $\alpha_{J^*}\leqslant1/2$, and otherwise set $J_1=(J^*)^c$. Then $2/5\leqslant\alpha_{J_1}\leqslant1/2$ and $1/2\leqslant\alpha_{J_1^c}\leqslant3/5$. Moreover, $|J_1^c|\geqslant2$, since we are not in case \emph{(i)}. It remains to partition $J_1^c$ into two sets $J_2$ and $J_3$ satisfying the required bounds. First suppose that there exists $j'\in J_1^c$ such that $\alpha_{j'}\geqslant1/10$. Then set $J_2=\{j'\}$ and $J_3=J_1^c\backslash J_2$. In this case $1/10\leqslant\alpha_{J_2}<2/5$, since we are not in case $(i)$, and
\[
  1/10<\alpha_{J_3}=\alpha_{J_1^c}-\alpha_{J_2}\leqslant1/2.
\]
Otherwise, $\alpha_j<1/10$ for all $j\in J_1^c$. Choose $J_2\subset J_1^c$ minimally such that $\sum_{j\in J_2}\alpha_j\geqslant1/10$ and set $J_3=J_1^c\backslash J_2$. Then $\alpha_{J_2}<1/5$ and hence
\[
  3/10<\alpha_{J_3}=\alpha_{J_1^c}-\alpha_{J_2}\leqslant1/2.
\]
This proves that case \emph{(iii)} always occurs when $(i)$ and $(ii)$ fail.

label: def:admissible-trilinear
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:admissible-trilinear}
  We call $a \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ an \emph{admissible trilinear component} if there exist exponents $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3 \in [1/10, 1/2]$ and functions $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3 \colon \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item We have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:admissible-trilinear-exponents}
 \frac1{10}\leqslant\gamma_2\leqslant\gamma_3\leqslant\gamma_1\leqslant\frac12,
 \qquad \gamma_1+\gamma_2+\gamma_3=1.
\end{equation}
and
  \[
  a=\alpha_1*\alpha_2*\alpha_3.
\]
\item The functions $\alpha_j$ are such that, for some $Z\asymp X$, we have
\[
 \operatorname{supp}(\alpha_j)
 \subseteq[Z^{\gamma_j},2Z^{\gamma_j}].
\]
Moreover, each $\alpha_j$ has the form
\[
 \alpha_j(n)=\1_{I_j}(n)(b_{j,1}*\cdots*b_{j,\ell_j})(n),
 \qquad I_j\subseteq[Z^{\gamma_j},2Z^{\gamma_j}],
\]
where $I_j$ is an interval, $\ell_1+\ell_2+\ell_3\leqslant20$, every $b_{j,r}$ is one of
\[
 \1_J,\qquad (\log \cdot)\1_J ,\qquad \mu\1_J
\]
for an interval $J\subseteq(N,2N]$, at most one of all the elementary factors is logarithmically weighted, and a M\"obius factor has $N\ll Z^{1/10}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: prop:HB-reduction
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:HB-reduction}
Each of the functions $\mu$ and $\Lambda$ admits a representation on $(X,X+H]$ as a linear combination of $O(\log^{O(1)} X)$ sums with coefficients satisfying $|a(n)|\ll d_{20}(n)\log X$ of the following forms.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \text{(Type I sums)}
We have $a=\alpha*\beta$, where
$$
  \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subset[1,X^{3/5}\log^{O(1)} X],
  \qquad
  \sum_{n\leqslant A}|\alpha(n)|^2\ll A\log^{O(1)} X
$$
for every $A \geqslant 1$, and the factor $\beta$ is a dyadic $1$-weighted or logarithmically weighted factor, and $\|\beta\|_{\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb N)}\ll\log^{O(1)} X$.
\item \text{(Type $I_2$ sums)}
We have $a=\alpha*\beta_1*\beta_2$, where
$$
  \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)
  \subset [1,X^{2/5}\log^{O(1)} X] \qquad
  \sum_{n\leqslant A}|\alpha(n)|^2\ll A\log^{O(1)} X,
$$
for every $A \geqslant 1$, and
$$
  \|\beta_1\|_{\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb N)} +\|\beta_2\|_{\operatorname{TV}(\mathbb N)} \ll\log^{O(1)} X.
$$
\item \text{(Type II sums)} We have $a=\alpha*\beta$, where $\textnormal{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq (M,2M]$, $\textnormal{supp}(\beta)\subseteq (N,2N]$ and
$$
 M,N\in  [X^{2/5}\log^{-O(1)} X, X^{3/5}\log^{O(1)} X],
$$
and moreover the coefficient sequences satisfy $\sum_{M < n\leqslant 2M}|\alpha(n)|^2\ll M\log^{O(1)} X$ and $\sum_{N < n \leqslant 2N}|\beta(n)|^{2k}\ll N\log^{O(1)} X$ for $k=1,2$.

Furthermore, every Type II component may be taken to be an admissible trilinear component.
\end{enumerate}

Furthermore, if we define
\[
 \Lambda_{X,\mathrm I}^{\sharp}(n)
 \coloneqq
 \frac{\mathcal P(R)}{\varphi(\mathcal P(R))}
 \sum_{\substack{d\leqslant X^{3/10}\\ d\mid(n,\mathcal P(R))}}\mu(d),
\]
then this function has a Type I representation as above and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cramer-type-I-error}
 \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}
 \left|\Lambda_X^\sharp(n)-\Lambda_{X,\mathrm I}^\sharp(n)\right|
 \ll H\exp\bigl(-c \log^{1/20} X\bigr).
\end{equation}

title: Proof
body_md: Apply the Heath-Brown identities for $\Lambda$ and $\mu$ in \cite[Lemma~2.16]{MSTT}, with $L=10$, and subdivide every factor dyadically. That lemma gives at most $20$ factors, each of type $\1_J$, $(\log \cdot)\1_J$, or $\mu\1_J$, with at most one logarithmic factor and with every M\"obius factor of length $\ll X^{1/10}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:comb3/5}, applied to the resulting support exponents and followed by a dyadic subdivision of each of the three grouped product variables, produces respectively the Type I alternative in Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction}\textup{(a)}, the Type $\mathrm I_2$ alternative in Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction}\textup{(b)}, and the admissible trilinear alternative in Definition~\ref{def:admissible-trilinear}, with the moment estimates following from the standard divisor bounds, while the assertion concerning $\Lambda_{X,\mathrm I}^{\sharp}$ and its error is \cite[(4.7)--(4.8)]{MSTT}.

label: prop:typeII-major
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:typeII-major}
Let $A,B\geqslant1$ and $\varepsilon>0$ be fixed. Let
$$
  X^{3/5+\varepsilon}\leqslant H\leqslant X^{1-\varepsilon},
$$
and let $a_n$ be any admissible trilinear component arising from Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction}\textup{(c)}. There is a constant $C_A=C(A,B,\varepsilon)>0$ such that, uniformly for
$$
 \frac{X}{H} \log^{C_A} X\leqslant |T|\leqslant X^B,
$$
one has
\begin{equation} \label{eq:MajorArc3/5claim}
  \left\lvert\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}a_n n^{iT}\right\rvert^{\,*} \ll_{A,B,\varepsilon} \frac{H}{\log^A X}.
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: High frequency trilinear major arcs at the $3/5$ scale

label: eq:typeII-major-progression
title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$P=\{b_0<n \leqslant b_0+L: n\equiv a \,(\mathrm{mod}\,q)\}\subseteq[X,X+H]$
be a progression on which the supremum in~\eqref{eq:starred-abs} is attained for~\eqref{eq:MajorArc3/5claim}. It suffices to show that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:typeII-major-progression}
\Big| \sum_{n \in P} a_n n^{iT}\Big|\ll_{A,B, \varepsilon } \frac{H}{\log^A X}.
\end{equation}
By the divisor bound, $a_n \ll_\varepsilon X^{\varepsilon/4}$, so that
\begin{equation*}
\sum_{n \in P} |a_n| \ll_{A,B, \varepsilon } X^{\varepsilon/4} \left(\frac{L}{q}+1\right).
\end{equation*}
This gives~\eqref{eq:typeII-major-progression} unless $L \geqslant H X^{-\varepsilon/2}$ and $q \leqslant X^{\varepsilon/2}$. 

Write $d=(a,q)$, $q=dq'$ and $a=da'$, so that $(a',q')=1$. Shiu's bound \cite[Theorem~1]{Shiu}, applied after $n=dm$, gives
\begin{align}\label{eq:shiu}
 \sum_{n\in P}|a_n|
 \ll \left(\frac{L}{d\varphi(q')}+1\right)d_{20}(d)\log^{O(1)} X \ll \frac{L}{q^{1/2}} \log^{O(1)} X.
\end{align}
It follows, on taking $A_1$ sufficiently large in terms of $A,B,\varepsilon$, that \eqref{eq:typeII-major-progression} holds if $L<H\log^{-A_1} X$ or $q>\log^{A_1} X$. We may therefore assume that
\[
L\geqslant H\log^{-A_1} X \quad \text{ and }\quad q\leqslant \log^{A_1} X.
\]

By the orthogonality of Dirichlet characters, we have
\begin{align}
\sum_{ \substack{ b_0<n \leqslant b_0+L \\ n \equiv a \,(\mathrm{mod}\,q)}} a_n n^{iT} &= \sum_{ \substack{ b_0<n \leqslant b_0+L \\ d \mid n \\ \frac{n}{d} \equiv a' \,(\mathrm{mod}\,q')}} a_{n} n^{iT}\nonumber\\
&= \frac{1}{ \varphi(q')} \sum_{\chi \,(\mathrm{mod}\,q')} \overline{\chi(a')}\sum_{\substack{b_0 <n \leqslant b_0+L \\ d \mid n}} a_{n} \chi(n/d) n^{iT}. \label{eq:dm}
\end{align}

Write $u_0=\lfloor b_0\rfloor+1/2$ and $v_0=\lfloor b_0+L\rfloor+1/2$, and let $T_1 \coloneqq \frac{X}{H}\log^{B_1} X$ with $B_1$ sufficiently large. The truncated Perron formula then gives
\begin{align}\begin{aligned}\label{eq:Perron}
\sum_{n}a_n\1_{d\mid n}\chi(n/d)n^{iT}\1_{[u_0,v_0]}(n)&=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{1/2-iT_1}^{1/2+iT_1}\frac{v_0^s-u_0^s}{s}\sum_{n}a_nn^{-s+iT}\1_{d\mid n}\chi(n/d)\,\textnormal{d} s\\
\quad &+ O\left(\frac{X}{T_1}\log^{O(1)} X+X^{o(1)}\right),
\end{aligned}
\end{align}
where the error bound follows from Shiu's bound after a dyadic subdivision by distance from the half-integer endpoints. Note that
\[
\frac{v_0^{1/2+it}-u_0^{1/2+it}}{1/2+it} \ll \frac{L}{X^{1/2}}.
\]

Fix a representation $a=\alpha_1*\alpha_2*\alpha_3$ and parameters
$Z,\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3$ as in
Definition~\ref{def:admissible-trilinear}.
For each factorisation $d_1d_2d_3=d$, set
\begin{align*}
 r_j&=\frac{d}{d_1\cdots d_j},\\
 \mathcal M_j(s)&=
 \sum_{\substack{d_j\mid n\\(n/d_j,r_j)=1}}
 \alpha_j(n)\chi(n/d_j)n^{-s+iT},
 \qquad 1\leqslant j\leqslant3.
\end{align*}
Note that the number of factorisations is $O(\log^{O_{A_1}(1)}X)$. Splitting the convolution variables successively according to
$d_1=(n_1,d)$ and $d_2=(n_2,d/d_1)$ yields
\begin{align*}
 \sum_{d\mid n}a_n\chi(n/d)n^{-s+iT}=
 \sum_{d_1d_2d_3=d}
 \mathcal M_1(s)\mathcal M_2(s)\mathcal M_3(s).
\end{align*}


The polynomials $\mathcal{M}_j(s)$ have supports on $[Z^{\gamma_j},2Z^{\gamma_j}]$ with the exponents in \eqref{eq:admissible-trilinear-exponents}. Thus, returning to~\eqref{eq:Perron}, we reduce matters to the normalised Dirichlet polynomial estimate, for some $A_2$ sufficiently large in terms of $A_1$, namely
\begin{equation}\label{eq:perron-reduction}
  \int_{-T_1}^{T_1}\left\lvert \mathcal M_1(1/2+it)\mathcal M_2(1/2+it)\mathcal M_3(1/2+it)\right\rvert\,\textnormal{d} t \ll_{A,B,\varepsilon} \frac{Z^{1/2}}{\log^{A_2} X},
\end{equation}
uniformly for all Dirichlet characters $\chi\pmod{q'}$ and all divisor allocations. If $C_A>B_1+2$, then for $|t|\leqslant T_1$,
\[
 Z^{\varepsilon/3}\leqslant |t-T|\leqslant Z^{B+1}.
\]

Recall that each $\alpha_j$ is a Dirichlet convolution of a bounded number of indicator sequences of intervals, or logarithmically weighted such indicators, or copies of M\"obius function. We open the elementary convolutions in the shortest factor $\mathcal M_2$. We distribute the divisibility condition among the elementary
variables by the same successive gcd decomposition and remove
the resulting coprimality conditions by M\"obius inversion.
This introduces only a polylogarithmic loss. One of the boundedly many factor polynomials has length $Z^{c+o(1)}$ for some $c=c(\varepsilon)>0$; after the other variables are fixed, it remains an interval sum with coefficient $1$, $\mu$ or $\log$ and a character of polylogarithmic modulus. Applying e.g. \cite[Lemma~3.9(i),(ii)]{MSTT} with $X = 2Z^{B+1}$  (and partial summation for $\log$) to that factor, and the trivial bound to the others, gives
$$
  \sup_{t\in [-T_1, T_1]}\left\lvert \mathcal M_2(1/2+it)\right\rvert \ll_{A,B,\varepsilon} Z^{\gamma_2/2} \log^{-A'} X
$$
for every $A'>0$. Moreover, $T_1\leqslant Z^{2/5-\varepsilon/3}$ for sufficiently large $X$, and the support and coefficient hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:BHP-trilinear-estimates} hold. Hence that lemma applies with $Z$ in place of $X$. Taking $A'$ sufficiently large gives \eqref{eq:perron-reduction}. This completes the proof.

title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Nilsequence discorrelation up to an abelian Type II obstruction

label: eq:absolute-mass-f
title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on the dimension of $G/\Gamma$. The zero-dimensional case is immediate, since a function with mean zero on a one-point nilmanifold vanishes.

Choose $C_0=C_0(d,D,A,\varepsilon)$ sufficiently large. On enlarging $C_0$, we may assume that it dominates all logarithmic powers in Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction}. Moreover, we may assume that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:absolute-mass-f}
 \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}|f(n)|\ll H\log^{C_0} X.
\end{equation}
Indeed, for $f=\mu$ this is immediate, while for $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_X^\sharp$ it follows from Shiu's bound and the definition of $\Lambda_X^\sharp$. Let $A_1$ be sufficiently large in terms of $d,D,A,\varepsilon,C_0$ to absorb any logarithmic losses that follow.

Choose $E>A+C_0+10$. By the Fourier decomposition of \cite[Proposition~2.9]{MSTT}, we have
\[
 F=\sum_{\xi\in\Xi}F_\xi+O(\log^{-E} X),\qquad |\Xi|+\max_{\xi\in\Xi}\|F_\xi\|_{\mathrm{Lip}}\ll \log^{O_{d,D,A,E}(1)} X,
\]
where $F_\xi$ oscillates with central frequency $\xi$. For each $\xi\in\Xi$, define
\[
 m_\xi=\int_{G/\Gamma}F_\xi,\qquad F_\xi^0=F_\xi-m_\xi.
\]
Then $F_\xi^0$ has mean zero; if $\xi\ne0$, Haar invariance gives $m_\xi=0$, while the zero-frequency component factors through the quotient by the centre. The error term is controlled by \eqref{eq:absolute-mass-f}, the constants $m_\xi$ by the major arc estimate of \cite[Theorem~3.1(i)]{MSTT}, and every component invariant under a positive-dimensional central subgroup by the induction hypothesis on the corresponding quotient. Consequently, after enlarging $A_1$, we may assume, unless the exceptional alternative has already occurred, that $\dim Z(G)=1$ and that $F$ oscillates with a non-zero central frequency.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction}, the function $f$ can be represented as a linear combination of $O(\log^{O(1)} X)$ functions $h$ of the following forms:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_1} X, X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I sum;
\item $h$ is a 	$(\log^{-A_1} X, X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})$ type I$_2$ sum;
\item $h$ is a $(\log^{-A_1} X, A_{II}^-,A_{II}^+)$ type II sum satisfying \begin{align} \label{eq:typeII-two-sided-range}
X^{2/5}\log^{-O(1)} X \ll A_{II}^{-}\leqslant A_{II}^{+}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}.
\end{align}
\end{enumerate}
For $f=\Lambda-\Lambda_X^\sharp$, the $L^1$ error in the last sentence of Proposition~\ref{prop:HB-reduction} is smaller than every required logarithmic loss. If the claimed discorrelation estimate fails, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform-nonabelian-bound2}
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^*\gg \frac{H}{ \log^{A+1} X}.
 \end{equation}
Then the triangle inequality and the number of components give one function $h$ of one of the above types for which
\begin{align}\label{eq:component_correlation}
\left| \sum_{X<n \leqslant X+H} h(n) F(g(n)\Gamma)\right|^* \gg \frac{H}{\log^{A+O(1)} X}.
\end{align}
We apply \cite[Theorem~4.2]{MSTT} to this component. In the Type I and Type $I_2$ cases, and in the non-abelian Type II case, it gives one of the following alternatives:
\begin{enumerate}
\item [\textbf{Case 1:}] a non-trivial horizontal character $\eta:G\to \mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of Lipschitz norm $O_{d,D}(\log^{O_{d,D,A,A_1}(1)} X)$ satisfies
\begin{align} \label{eq:horiz-charac}
\|\eta \circ g\|_{C^\infty [X,X+H]} \ll_{d,D} \log^{O_{A_1}(1)} X;	
\end{align}
\item[\textbf{Case 2:}] the component $h$ is Type II and the nilmanifold is abelian.
\end{enumerate}
The size alternative in \cite[Theorem~4.2(i),(ii),(iv)]{MSTT} cannot occur. Indeed, the corresponding quantities in the three cases satisfy
\[
 X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}=o(H),\qquad X^{1/3}(X^{2/5+\varepsilon/5})^{2/3}=X^{3/5+2\varepsilon/15}=o(H),
\]
and, by \eqref{eq:typeII-two-sided-range},
\[
 \max\{A_{II}^+,X/A_{II}^-\}\ll X^{3/5+\varepsilon/5}\log^{O(1)} X=o(H).
\]

In Case~2, since $\dim Z(G)=1$, the group $G$ is one-dimensional. The single-frequency property therefore gives
\[
F(g(n)\Gamma)=b\,e(P(n))
\]
for some $b\in\mathbb C$ and some polynomial $P:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R$ of degree at most $d$. The original failed correlation~\eqref{eq:uniform-nonabelian-bound2} and the component correlation~\eqref{eq:component_correlation} give now
\begin{align}
\left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)e(P(n))\right|^*&\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_1} X,
                                              \label{eq:original-poly-correlation}\\
  \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)e(P(n))\right|^*&\gg_{d,D,A,\varepsilon}H\log^{-A_1} X.
 \label{eq:component-poly-correlation}
\end{align}
After normalising by $b$, \cite[Theorem~4.2(iii)]{MSTT} gives an integer $q\ll \log^{O_{A_1}(1)} X$ and a number $ |T| \leqslant (X/H)^{d+1} \log^{O_{A_1}(1)} X$ such that
\begin{align}
    \|e(P(n))n^{-iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb Z;q)} &\ll_{d,D,A,\varepsilon} \log^{O(A_1)} X,
 \label{eq:poly-twist}
\end{align}
By \cite[Lemma~2.2(iii)]{MSTT}, combining~\eqref{eq:original-poly-correlation} and \eqref{eq:component-poly-correlation} with \eqref{eq:poly-twist} and enlarging $A_1$ give~\eqref{eq:original-mult-correlation} and  \eqref{eq:component-multiplicative-correlation}. This is the exceptional alternative in the statement.
 
 
Therefore, it remains to consider the case in which \eqref{eq:horiz-charac} holds. As in \cite[Section~4.2]{MSTT}, we apply \cite[Lemma~2.11]{MSTT} to factor $g\in\operatorname{Poly}(\mathbb Z\to G)$ as $g=\varepsilon g'\gamma$, where $\varepsilon$ is smooth, $\gamma$ is rational and $g'\in\operatorname{Poly}(\mathbb Z,\ker\eta)$. Freezing $\varepsilon$ and $\gamma$ incurs an error of $O(H \log^{-A-1} X)$ and splits $(X,X+H]$ into $O(\log^{O_{A_1}(1)} X)$ arithmetic progressions $P_j$, as in \cite[Section~4.2]{MSTT}. On each $P_j$, we are therefore reduced to a nilsequence $F_j(g_j(n)\Gamma_j)$ on a proper rational subnilmanifold $G_j/\Gamma_j$ satisfying $\dim G_j<\dim G$.


With the constants in this factorisation fixed, choose $B'$ sufficiently large in terms of $A_1,A,d,D,\varepsilon$ to absorb the number of progressions and all other logarithmic losses. If the induction hypothesis, applied to the mean-zero part of some $F_j$ on the original interval $(X,X+H]$, yields its exceptional alternative, then it gives \eqref{eq:original-mult-correlation} and \eqref{eq:component-multiplicative-correlation}, together with the required bound for $T$, with a possibly larger logarithmic exponent. We enlarge the final value of $A_1$ to that exponent. Otherwise, after subtracting the mean of $F_j$, the major arc estimate and the induction hypothesis, both applied with saving exponent $B'$, give
\[
\Big|\sum_{n\in P_j}f(n)F_j(g_j(n)\Gamma_j)\Big|^{*}\ll \frac{H}{\log^{B'} X}.
\]
Intersecting an arbitrary arithmetic progression with the $P_j$ and summing the resulting estimates gives
\[
\Big|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)F(g(n)\Gamma)\Big|^{*}\ll \frac{H}{\log^A X},
\]
as claimed. This completes the induction and hence the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $f\in\{\mu,\Lambda-\Lambda_X^\sharp\}$. Subtracting the mean of
$F$, the constant part is bounded by \cite[Theorem~3.1(i)]{MSTT};
thus we may suppose that $F$ has mean zero. The Lipschitz norm of the new $F$ is at most $2/\delta$. Fix a sufficiently large
$M=M(A,d,D)$, and write
\[
 A'=\max\{A,M+1\}.
\]
If $\delta<\log^{-M} X$, the trivial estimate
\[
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}
 f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^*
 \ll\delta^{-1}H\log X
\]
is at most $\delta^{-O_{d,D}(1)} H \log^{-A} X$ once the exponent
implicit in $O_{d,D}(1)$ is chosen sufficiently large. If
$\delta\geqslant\log^{-M} X$, the complexity of $G/\Gamma$ is at most
$\log^M X$. We apply Proposition~\ref{prop:non-abelian}
to $\overline F$ with $A'$ in place of $A$. We reach
\[
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}
 f(n)\overline{F(g(n)\Gamma)}\right|^*
 \ll_{d, D, A, \varepsilon} \frac{H}{\log^{A'} X}\ll \frac{H}{\log^A X},
\]
unless the alternative of that proposition holds.

It remains to rule out the alternative of
Proposition~\ref{prop:non-abelian}. Let $h,T$ and $A_1$ be as
there. We apply Proposition~\ref{prop:typeII-major} with $A_1+10$ and $d+2$ in place of $A$ and $B$
and let $C_2=C_2(A_1+10,d+2,\varepsilon)$ be the constant denoted $C_A$ there.
If
\[
 \frac{X}{H} \log^{C_2} X\leqslant |T|
 \leqslant \left(\frac{X}{H}\right)^{d+1}\log^{A_1} X,
\]
then $|T|\leqslant X^{d+2}$ for all sufficiently large $X$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:typeII-major} gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}h(n)n^{iT}\right|^*
 \ll \frac{H}{\log^{A_1+10} X},
\]
contradicting \eqref{eq:component-multiplicative-correlation}.

Suppose instead that
\[
 |T|<\frac{X}{H} \log^{C_2} X.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:variation-nit}
 \|n^{iT}\|_{\mathrm{TV}((X,X+H]\cap\mathbb Z)}
 \ll 1+  \sum_{\substack{X<n \leqslant X+H}}
 |(n+1)^{iT}-n^{iT}|\ll 1+ |T| \frac{H}{X}
 \ll\log^{C_2} X.
\end{equation}
Combining this with~\eqref{eq:original-mult-correlation} and
\cite[Lemma~2.2(iii)]{MSTT}, we obtain
\[
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}f(n)\right|^*
 \gg \frac{H}{\log^{A_1+C_2} X}.
\]
The major arc estimate of \cite[Theorem~3.1(i)]{MSTT}, applied with
saving exponent $A_1+C_2+1$, contradicts this. Hence the alternative
in Proposition~\ref{prop:non-abelian} cannot occur, and the theorem
follows.

label: lem:combHBI
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:combHBI}
Let $\tau \in (0, 1/2)$, let $0\leqslant\eta<1-2\tau$, and let $k\geqslant 1$. Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k\geqslant0$, write $S=\sum_{j\leqslant k}\alpha_j$, and suppose that $|S-1|\leqslant\eta$. For $J\subset\{1,\ldots,k\}$ write $\alpha_J=\sum_{j\in J}\alpha_j$. Then at least one of the following alternatives holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item There is an index $j_0 \in \{1, \dotsc, k\}$ such that $\alpha_{j_0} > \tau$.
\item There is a partition $\{1, \dotsc, k\} = J_1 \sqcup J_2$ with $\alpha_{J_1}, \alpha_{J_2} \in [\tau, S-\tau].$
\item There is an index $j_0 \in \{1, \dotsc, k\}$ and a partition $\{1, \dotsc, k\} =\{j_0\} \sqcup J_1\sqcup J_2$ such that $S-2\tau<\alpha_{j_0}\leqslant\tau$ and, for $r \in \{1, 2\}$, we have
\[
 S-2\tau<\alpha_{J_r}< \tau.
\]
\end{enumerate}

name: Type I, Type II, Type I/II trichotomy

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that \emph{(i)} and \emph{(ii)} fail. After discarding zero terms, choose maximal disjoint sets $J_1,J_2\subseteq\{1,\dotsc,k\}$ such that $\alpha_{J_1},\alpha_{J_2}<\tau$. Write $J_0=\{1,\dotsc,k\}\setminus(J_1\cup J_2)$.

  Let us first show that $|J_0|=1$. Since $S\geqslant 2\tau$, we have $J_0\neq\emptyset$. Assume for contradiction that there exist distinct $r_1,r_2\in J_0$. By maximality,
$$
\alpha_{J_1 \cup \{r_1\}}, \alpha_{J_2 \cup \{r_2\}} \geqslant \tau.
$$
Since we are not in case \emph{(ii)}, neither sum lies in $[\tau,S-\tau]$, so both exceed $S-\tau$. But then
\[
S \geqslant \alpha_{J_1 \cup \{r_1\}} + \alpha_{J_2 \cup \{r_2\}} > 2(S-\tau) \geqslant S,
\]
which is a contradiction. Hence $|J_0|=1$, so $J_0=\{j_0\}$ for some $j_0\in \{1,\ldots, k\}$.

Since case \emph{(i)} fails, $\alpha_{j_0}\leqslant\tau$. Moreover, neither $J_1$ nor $J_2$ is empty, since otherwise $S<2\tau$. We have
\[
 \alpha_{j_0}=S-\alpha_{J_1}-\alpha_{J_2}>S-2\tau,
\]
and, for $\{r,s\}=\{1,2\}$,
\[
 \alpha_{J_r}=S-\alpha_{j_0}-\alpha_{J_s}>S-2\tau.
\]
Thus if $(i)$ and $(ii)$ fail, we are indeed in case \emph{(iii)}.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $H>Y$, the Vinogradov--Korobov estimate for the summatory M\"obius function gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)\right|\ll X\exp\bigl(-c\log^{3/5} X(\log\log X)^{-1/5}\bigr)
 \ll \frac{H}{\log^{100} X},
\]
so there is nothing to prove. We may therefore assume that $H\leqslant Y$.

Choose $B_0 = 100$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:ramare-component-comparison} to compensate for the $O(\log^{2K+2} X)$ dyadic components. Summing \eqref{eq:ramare-component-comparison} and recombining Heath-Brown's identity and~\eqref{eq:ramare-identity-section2} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mobius-recombined-long}
  \sum_{X<n\leqslant X+H}\mu(n)
  =\frac{H}{Y}\sum_{X<n\leqslant X+Y}\mu(n)+O_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{H}{\log^{1/3-\varepsilon} X}\right).
\end{equation}
For some $c>0$, the main term on the right-hand side is $\ll H\exp(-c\log^{3/5} X(\log\log X)^{-1/5})$ by the classical zero-free region for $\zeta(s)$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:intro-mobius} follows.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $A>B_0$ sufficiently large in terms of $K = 20$ to absorb the fixed logarithmic losses in this proof.

For $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$, write
\[
\beta_j = \max\left\{\frac{\log N_j}{\log X}, 0\right\},\qquad \beta_{2K} = \max\left\{\frac{\log R}{\log X}, 0\right\},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{\log P_1}{\log X},
\]
and set $S=\sum_{j=1}^{2K}\beta_j$. By \eqref{eq:product-dyadic-lengths},
\[
 S=1-\rho+O(1/\log X),\qquad 0\leqslant\rho\leqslant\frac{1}{(\log\log X)^2}+O(1/\log X).
\]
Thus, for $X$ sufficiently large, Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI} applies to $\beta_1,\dotsc,\beta_{2K}$ with
\[
 \tau=\frac{16}{35}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4},\qquad
 \eta=\frac{2}{(\log\log X)^2}.
\]

We split into cases.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Case 1: Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI}(i) holds.}
Now there is an index $j_0$ with $\beta_{j_0}>\tau.$ Since $\tau > 2/K$, $\alpha_{j_0}$ is an interval indicator. Write its supporting interval as $I_{j_0}=(u,v]$. Putting the sum over $n_{j_0}$ inside, in this case we obtain, for some $|b_m| \leqslant d_{100}(m)$,
\[
 S_{(X,X+H]} - \frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]} = \sum_{m \leqslant 2X/N_{j_0}} b_m \left(\sum_{\substack{X/m < n_{j_0} \leqslant (X+H)/m \\ n_{j_0} \in (u, v]}} 1 - \frac{H}{Y} \sum_{\substack{X/m < n_{j_0} \leqslant (X+Y)/m \\ n_{j_0} \in (u, v]}} 1\right).
  \]
Now the difference in the parentheses is $O(1)$ unless
\[
 X<mu\leqslant X+Y\qquad\text{or}\qquad X<mv\leqslant X+Y.
\]
There are $O(Y/N_{j_0}+1)$ integers $m$ for which one of these holds, and for each of them the difference in the parentheses is $O(1+HN_{j_0}/X) = O(HN_{j_0}/X)$. Shiu's bound for the divisor bounded coefficients $b_m$ thus gives
\[
S_{(X,X+H]} - \frac{H}{Y}S_{(X,X+Y]} \ll \left(\frac{X}{N_{j_0}} + \frac{HY}{X} + \frac{HN_{j_0}}{X} \right) \log^{O(1)}X.
\]
Since $N_{j_0}\in (X^\tau, 2X/P]$, $H\geqslant X^{19/35+\varepsilon}$, and $Y/X=\exp(-3\log^{1/3} X)$, this is $\ll_{A,\varepsilon} H/\log^A X$ as claimed.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2: Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI}(ii) or (iii) holds.}
By a standard reduction using Perron's formula (see e.g.~\cite[Lemma 7.2]{HarmanBook}), it is enough to prove that, for every $A \geqslant 1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:perron-target-section2}
  \int_{T_0}^{T_1}\left|P_1(1/2+it)N_{2K}(1/2+it)\prod_{j=1}^{2K-1} N_j(1/2+it)\right|\,\textnormal{d} t\ll_A \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^A X},
\end{equation}
where
\[
 T_0=\exp(\log^{1/3} X),\qquad T_1=\frac{X^{1+\varepsilon/2}}{H} \leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2},
\]
and
\[
 P_1(s)=\sum_{P_1<p\leqslant \min\{2P_1,Q\}}p^{-s},\quad N_{2K}(s)=\sum_{R<r\leqslant2R}a_r r^{-s},\quad N_j(s)=\sum_{N_j<n\leqslant2N_j}\alpha_j(n)n^{-s}
\]
for $1\leqslant j\leqslant 2K-1$.


\medskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2.1: Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI}(ii) holds.}
Let $J_1\sqcup J_2=\{1,\dotsc,2K\}$ be the partition in the lemma and set, for $\ell \in \{1, 2\}$,
\[
A_\ell(s)=\prod_{j\in J_\ell}N_j(s),
\]
and
\begin{equation*}
 \beta_{J_\ell}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in J_\ell}\beta_j,
\end{equation*}
so that $A_\ell(s)$ has length $X^{\beta_{J_\ell}}$.

Alternative \emph{(ii)} of Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:case2-product-lengths}
 \tau\leqslant\beta_{J_1},\beta_{J_2}\leqslant S-\tau.
\end{equation}
Since $\tau=\frac{16}{35}-\frac{\varepsilon}{4}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:case2-lengths-exceed-T}
T_1\leqslant X^{16/35-\varepsilon/2}=X^{\tau-\varepsilon/4} \leqslant \min\{X^{\beta_{J_1}}, X^{\beta_{J_2}}\}.
\end{equation}
 For every $B_0>0$, by the zero-free region estimate in the form used in \cite[Lemma~4.3]{MatomakiTeravainenMobius}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{P1}
	\sup_{T_0\leqslant|t|\leqslant T_1}|P_1(1/2+it)|\ll_{B_0} P_1^{1/2}\log^{-B_0} X.
\end{equation}

The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, followed by the mean-value theorem for Dirichlet polynomials  (see e.g.~\cite[Theorem 9.1]{IwaniecKowalski}),~\eqref{eq:case2-lengths-exceed-T}, and~\eqref{eq:product-dyadic-lengths} yields
\begin{align*}
 &\int_{T_0}^{T_1}
 |P_1(1/2+it)A_1(1/2+it)A_2(1/2+it)|\,\,\textnormal{d} t\\
 &\ll_{B_0} P_1^{1/2} \log^{-B_0} X\left(\int_{T_0}^{T_1}|A_1(1/2+it)|^2\,\,\textnormal{d} t
 \right)^{1/2}\left(\int_{T_0}^{T_1}|A_2(1/2+it)|^2\,\,\textnormal{d} t\right)^{1/2}\\
  &\ll P_1^{1/2}\log^{-B_0} X\left(T_1 + X^{\beta_{J_1}}\right)^{1/2}\left(T_1 + X^{\beta_{J_2}}\right)^{1/2} \log^{O(1)} X\\
 &\ll P_1^{1/2}(X^{\beta_{J_1}+\beta_{J_2}})^{1/2}\log^{-B_0+O(1)} X \ll \frac{X^{1/2}}{\log^{B_0-O(1)} X}
\end{align*}
Choosing $B_0$ sufficiently large therefore gives~\eqref{eq:perron-target-section2}.

\medskip\noindent\textbf{Case 2.2: Lemma~\ref{lem:combHBI}(iii) holds.}
Let $\{1,\dotsc,2K\}=\{j_0\}\sqcup J_1\sqcup J_2$ be the partition in the lemma, and set $\beta_{J_r}=\sum_{j\in J_r}\beta_j$. Then
\[
 S-2\tau<\beta_{j_0},\beta_{J_1},\beta_{J_2}\leqslant\tau.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 S-2\tau=\frac3{35}+\frac\varepsilon2-\rho+O(1/\log X)>\frac1K
\]
for sufficiently large $X$. Hence $j_0\leqslant K-1$, so $N_{j_0}(s)$ is an interval-indicator factor. Absorb $P_1(s)$ into either of the other two blocks and subdivide the two product supports into $O_K(1)$ dyadic pieces. For a fixed piece, write the product as $L(s)M(s)N(s)$, with $L(s)=N_{j_0}(s)$, let $L_0,M_0,N_0$ be the lengths of the polynomials, and set $\widetilde X=L_0M_0N_0\asymp_KX$. Writing
\[
  L_0 = \widetilde{X}^{\gamma_1}, \quad   M_0 =\widetilde{X}^{\gamma_2}, \quad   N_0 = \widetilde{X}^{\gamma_3},
  \]
we have $\gamma_1, \gamma_2, \gamma_3 \in [\varepsilon/8,16/35-\varepsilon/8]$ with $\gamma_1 + \gamma_2 + \gamma_3 = 1$. Furthermore, for sufficiently large $X$,
\[
T_1\leqslant\widetilde X^{16/35-\varepsilon/8}, \qquad T_0\geqslant\exp(\log^{1/4}\widetilde X).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:hbi-trilinear-estimates}, applied with $\widetilde X$ in place of $X$ and $\varepsilon/8$ in place of $\varepsilon$, now gives \eqref{eq:perron-target-section2}.

label: eq:16/35-reduc-tau1
title: Proof
body_md:
First of all, we observe that $H_{j,\tau}(\nu)$ is nondecreasing in $\tau\in [\varepsilon, \tau_1]$. As a consequence, $\{ \nu: H_{j,\tau}(\nu) \geqslant t\}\subseteq \{ \nu: H_{j,\tau_1} (\nu) \geqslant t\}$. From the definition of $P_{j,\tau}$ in Lemma~\ref{le:16/35comput} we thus have for $\tau\in [\varepsilon, \tau_1]$ and $0\leqslant t \leqslant \tau$ that
\[
P_{j,\tau}(t) \geqslant P_{j,\tau_1}(t).
\] 
For convenience, set $P_j(t) =P_{j,\tau_1}(t)$ and $R_\beta(t) =R_{\beta,\tau_1}(t)$. It then suffices to prove that 
\begin{align} \label{eq:16/35-reduc-tau1}
F(t) := P_1(t) + P_2(t) + P_3(t) -t > \varepsilon^{10}
\end{align}
for all $0\leqslant t\leqslant \tau_1$.

Since $\nu$ takes values in the interval $[\varepsilon^6,\varepsilon^{-1}]$, we can conclude the above inequality when $t$ is rather small. Indeed, for all $t \in [0, \tau_1]$ one has
  \[
    P_1(t) + P_2(t) + P_3(t) \geqslant(\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3)\varepsilon^6 = \varepsilon^6.
    \]
Thus, for $t \leqslant \varepsilon^6/2$, we have
\[
F(t)\geqslant \frac{\varepsilon^6}{2}>\varepsilon^{10}.
\]

Let us assume below that $\varepsilon^6/2< t\leqslant \tau_1$. From the definition of $R_\beta(t)$, it is immediate that if $\mathcal K(\beta_2,\nu;\tau_1) \geqslant t$ and $\mathcal K(2\beta_2,\nu;\tau_1)\geqslant t$, then $\beta_2\nu \geqslant R_{\beta_2}(t)$ and $2\beta_2\nu \geqslant R_{2\beta_2}(t)$. Thus it follows from the definitions of $P_2(t)$ in Lemma~\ref{le:16/35comput} and $R_{\beta}(t)$ in~\eqref{eq:Rbetadef} that
\begin{align}\label{eq:BHPPjlower-p2}
P_2(t) \geqslant \max\left\{R_{\beta_2}(t), \frac{1}{2} R_{2\beta_2}(t)\right\}.	
\end{align}
Similarly,
\begin{align} \label{eq:BHPPjlower}
 P_3(t) \geqslant \max\left\{R_{\beta_3}(t), \frac{1}{2} R_{2\beta_3}(t)\right\}, \qquad
  P_1(t) \geqslant \max\left\{\frac{t-\tau_1+2\beta_1}{4}, \frac{1}{2} R_{2\beta_1}(t)\right\}.
\end{align}
We shall prove~\eqref{eq:16/35-reduc-tau1} for $t \in [\varepsilon^6/2,\tau_1]$ using these piecewise-linear lower
bounds.

We first make a preliminary reduction. By~\eqref{eq:BHPPjlower}, \eqref{eq:BHPPjlower-p2} and \eqref{eq:Rbetadef}, we have, for $\beta_2, \beta_3 \leqslant \tau_1$, 
\begin{align*}
  P_1(t) + P_2(t) + P_3(t) &\geqslant \frac{t-\tau_1+2\beta_1}{4} + \min\left\{\frac{t}{4}, \frac{t-\tau_1+2\beta_2}{4}\right\} + \frac{t-\tau_1+\beta_3}{2} \\
  &= \min\left\{t-\frac{3}{4}\tau_1+\frac{\beta_1+\beta_3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}+t-\tau_1\right\}.
\end{align*}
The second term in the minimum is $t+3/70+\varepsilon>t+\varepsilon^{10}$. The first term is strictly greater than $t+\varepsilon^{10}$ if
\[
  \beta_1+\beta_3 > \frac{3}{2}\tau_1+2\varepsilon^{10} \iff \beta_2 < 1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_1-2\varepsilon^{10}.
  \]
  Thus, using also the symmetry between $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$, we may restrict ourselves to the case
  \[
    \beta_2, \beta_3 \in \left[1-\frac{3}{2}\tau_1-2\varepsilon^{10}, \tau_1\right] \subseteq [11/35 +\varepsilon,\tau_{1}].
    \]
In particular, after interchanging $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$ if necessary, we assume from now on that
\[
  \frac{11}{35} +\varepsilon \leqslant \beta_2\leqslant \beta_3 \leqslant \tau_1.
\]
Since $\varepsilon \in (0, 1/100)$, we have $11/35+\varepsilon \geqslant \tau_1/2$, so $\beta_2,\beta_3\geqslant \tau_1/2$ in this range. When $\beta \geqslant \tau_1 /2$ let
 \begin{align}\label{eq:end-slope}
 p(\beta) =\beta -\tau_1/2	
 \end{align}
denote the first breakpoint of~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulowmid} and~\eqref{eq:Rbtauupmid}, thus the end of the initial slope-$1/2$ segment. Similarly let
\begin{align}\label{eq:return-slope}
 r(\beta) = 
 \begin{cases}
   \tau_1 -2\beta/5, \qquad &\text{ if } \beta \leqslant 5\tau_1/6;\\
 	3\tau_1/2 -\beta, &\text{ if } 5\tau_1/6 \leqslant \beta \leqslant \tau_1,
 \end{cases}	
\end{align}
denote the last breakpoint of~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulow},~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulowmid} and~\eqref{eq:Rbtauupmid}, thus the beginning of the final slope-$1/2$ segment. Then $r(\beta)$ is a continuous and non-increasing function in $\beta$. Since $R_{\beta_2}(t) =R_{\beta_3} (t) =t/2$ whenever $0\leqslant t \leqslant p(\beta_2)\leqslant p(\beta_3)$, we then have
\[
F(t) \geqslant P_1(t) \geqslant \beta_1 \varepsilon^6 \geqslant \varepsilon^7>\varepsilon^{10},
\]
as desired.

It therefore remains to consider the case $p(\beta_2) \leqslant t \leqslant \tau_1$. We divide the rest of the argument into two cases depending on whether $\beta_1\geqslant\tau_1/2$ or $\beta_1 < \tau_1/2$. 

\textbf{Case 1: $\beta_1\geqslant \tau_1/2$}. 
Define
\[
  F_{+}(t) = R_{\beta_2}(t) + R_{\beta_3}(t) + \frac{t-\tau_1+2\beta_1}{4} -t.
\]
From~\eqref{eq:BHPPjlower-p2}--\eqref{eq:BHPPjlower}, it suffices to show that $F_{+}(t) > \varepsilon^{10}$ whenever $t \in [p(\beta_2),\tau_1]$. We shall show that $F_+(t)$ attains its minimum at $t = r(\beta_2)$.

When $t \in [p(\beta_2), r(\beta_2)]$, the slope of $R_{\beta_2}$ is at most $1/4$, and the slope of $R_{\beta_3}$ is at most $1/2$. Therefore the slope of $F_+(t)$ is at most $0$.
On the other hand, when $t\geqslant r(\beta_2) \geqslant r(\beta_3)$ both $R_{\beta_2}$ and $R_{\beta_3}$ are on their final branches (noting $r(\beta)$ is non-increasing), hence both of them have slope $1/2$. Thus in this range $F_+$ has slope
\[
1/2+1/2+1/4-1=1/4 \geqslant 0.
\]
Consequently, $F_{+}$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_2)$, and the minimum is
\begin{align*}
  F_+(r(\beta_2)) &= \frac{r(\beta_2)-\tau_1+\beta_2}{2} + \frac{r(\beta_2)-\tau_1+\beta_3}{2}+\frac{r(\beta_2)-\tau_1+2\beta_1}{4}-r(\beta_2) \\
  &= \frac{r(\beta_2)}{4}-\frac{5}{4}\tau_1+\frac{1}{2}.
\end{align*}
If $\beta_2\leqslant 5\tau_1/6$, then $r(\beta_2) =\tau_1-2\beta_2/5$ and therefore,
\[
F_{+} (r(\beta_2)) =  -\tau_1 -\frac{\beta_2}{10} + \frac12
\geqslant \frac12-\frac{13\tau_1}{12}
>\varepsilon^{10},
\]
If instead $\beta_2> 5\tau_1/6$, then $r(\beta_{2})=\frac{3\tau_{1}}{2}-\beta_{2}$. Using also $\beta_2\leqslant(1-\beta_1)/2\leqslant1/2-\tau_1/4$, we obtain
\[
F_{+} (r(\beta_2)) = \frac12 -\frac{7\tau_1}{8} - \frac{\beta_2}{4}
\geqslant\frac38-\frac{13\tau_1}{16}
>\varepsilon^{10}.
\]
This proves~\eqref{eq:16/35-reduc-tau1} in Case~1.

\textbf{Case 2: $\beta_1 < \tau_1/2$}.
Define
\[
  F_{-} (t) = R_{\beta_2}(t) + R_{\beta_3}(t) + R_{2\beta_1}(t)/2 -t.
\]
For $t \in [p(\beta_2),r(\beta_2)]$, the slopes of $R_{\beta_2}$, $R_{\beta_3}$, and $R_{2\beta_1}/2$ are at most $1/4$, $1/2$, and $1/4$, respectively, so the slope of $F_-$ is $\leqslant 0$ in this interval. For $t \in [r(\beta_2),\tau_1]$, the first two slopes equal $1/2$ and the slope of $R_{2\beta_1}$ is non-negative, so the slope of $F_-$ is $\geqslant 0$ in this interval. Therefore $F_-$ attains its minimum at $r(\beta_2)$, and the minimum is
\begin{align*}
  F_{-} (r(\beta_2)) &= \frac{r(\beta_2)-\tau_1+\beta_2}{2} + \frac{r(\beta_2)-\tau_1+\beta_3}{2}+\frac{R_{2\beta_1} (r(\beta_2))}{2}-r(\beta_2)\\
  &= \frac12 -\frac{\beta_1}{2}-\tau_1 +\frac{R_{2\beta_1} (r(\beta_2))}{2}.
\end{align*}

Thus it suffices to show that
\begin{align}\label{eq:claim-beta1}
 R_{2\beta_1} (r(\beta_2)) > 2\tau_1+\beta_1-1+2\varepsilon^{10}
\end{align}
Consider this for a fixed $\beta_1 < \tau_1/2$. Now $R_{2\beta_1}(t)$ is increasing in $t$ while $r(\beta_2)$ is decreasing in $\beta_2$. Thus $R_{2\beta_1}(r(\beta_2))$ is minimal when $\beta_2$ is maximal. Since $\beta_2 \leqslant \beta_3$ and $\beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 = 1$, we have $\beta_2 \leqslant (1-\beta_1)/2$. Thus it suffices to show~\eqref{eq:claim-beta1} for $\beta_2 = (1-\beta_1)/2$. For $\beta_1 < \tau_1/2$, we have $(1-\beta_1)/2 \geqslant 5\tau_1/6$. Thus, by definition of $r(\beta)$ it suffices to show that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:R2bet1bound}
 H(\beta_1) := R_{2\beta_1}\left(\frac{3\tau_1}{2}+\frac{\beta_1-1}{2}\right) - (2\tau_1+\beta_1-1+2\varepsilon^{10}) > 0.
\end{equation} 
Looking carefully at~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulow},~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulowmid},~\eqref{eq:Rbtauupmid},~\eqref{eq:Rbtauup}, we see that the slope of $H(\beta_1)$ is $\leqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_1}$ is $< r(2\beta_1)$ and $\geqslant 0$ when the argument of $R_{2\beta_1}$ is $\geqslant r(2 \beta_1)$. Thus it suffices to consider the case
  \begin{equation} \label{eq:r2beta1eq}
    \frac{3\tau_1}{2}+\frac{\beta_1-1}{2} = r(2\beta_1)
  \end{equation}
  
    If we had $2 \beta_1 \leqslant 5\tau_1/6$, it would follow that
  \[
    r(2\beta_1) = \tau_1 - \frac{4\beta_1}{5}.
  \]
In this case
\[
  \frac{3\tau_1}{2}+\frac{\beta_1-1}{2} - r(2\beta_1) = \frac{\tau_1}{2} -\frac{1}{2} +\frac{13}{10}\beta_1 \leqslant \frac{25}{24}\tau_1 - \frac{1}{2} < 0.
  \]
Thus~\eqref{eq:r2beta1eq} does not have a solution with $2\beta_1 \leqslant 5\tau_1/6$ and $H(\beta_1)$ is non-increasing in this range.

For $2 \beta_1 > 5\tau_1/6$, by the definition of $r(\beta)$,
    \[
    \frac{3\tau_1}{2}+\frac{\beta_1-1}{2} = \frac{3\tau_1}{2} - 2\beta_1 \iff \beta_1 = \frac{1}{5}
  \]
  and
  \[
    R_{2/5}\left(\frac{3\tau_1}{2}+\frac{\frac{1}{5}-1}{2}\right) = \frac{\frac{3\tau_1}{2}-\frac{2}{5}-\tau_1+\frac{2}{5}}{2} = \frac{\tau_1}{4}. 
  \]
  Thus
  \[
    H(1/5) = \frac{\tau_1}{4}-(2\tau_1 + \frac{1}{5} -1 + 2\varepsilon^{10}) = -\frac{7\tau_1}{4} + \frac{4}{5} -2\varepsilon^{10}.
  \]
  Recalling $\tau_1 = 16/35-\varepsilon$, we see that $H(1/5) = \frac{7}{4}\varepsilon-2\varepsilon^{10}> 0$ and the claim follows.

label: eq:3/5-reduc-tau1
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\tau^*=2/5-\varepsilon$ and, for convenience, set $P_\beta(t) =P_{\beta,\tau^\ast}(t)$ and $R_\beta(t) =R_{\beta,\tau^\ast}(t)$. Arguing as in the beginning of the proof of Lemma~\ref{le:16/35comput}, it suffices to show that
  \begin{align} \label{eq:3/5-reduc-tau1}
F(t) := P_{\beta_1}(t) + P_{\beta_2}(t) + P_{\beta_3}(t) -t > \varepsilon^{10}
\end{align}
for all $t\in [\varepsilon^6/2, \tau^\ast]$. Note that, for all $\beta \in \{\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3\}$,
\begin{equation} \label{eq:Pbetatlow3/5}
P_\beta(t) \geqslant \max \Big\{R_{\beta} (t), \frac{R_{2\beta} (t)}{2}\Big\}.
\end{equation}
We may assume that $\beta_2\leqslant\beta_3$. Since
$\beta_2\geqslant1/5$ and $\beta_1\geqslant2/5$, we have
$\beta_1,2\beta_2\geqslant\tau^*$. We therefore deduce from~\eqref{eq:Pbetatlow3/5} and the definition
of $R_\beta(t)$ that 
\[
P_{\beta_1} (t) \geqslant R_{\beta_1}(t)=\frac{t}{2} \qquad \text{ and }\qquad P_{\beta_2}(t) \geqslant \frac{R_{2\beta_2} (t)}{2}=\frac{t}{4}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
P_{\beta_1}(t) + P_{\beta_2} (t) + P_{\beta_3} (t) -t \geqslant P_{\beta_3} (t) -\frac{t}{4}\geqslant R_{\beta_3}(t)-\frac{t}{4}.
\]
The remaining task is to prove that for all $t\in [\varepsilon^6/2, \tau^*]$ we have
\begin{align} \label{eq:function-T}
R_{\beta_3}(t)-\frac{t}{4} > \varepsilon^{10}.
\end{align}
First of all, we notice that
\begin{equation} \label{eq:beta3simplow}
  \beta_3\geqslant (1-\beta_1)/2 \geqslant 1/4\geqslant \tau^*/2.
\end{equation}
If $R_{\beta_3}(t)=t/2$, then~\eqref{eq:function-T} is immediate. In particular we can concentrate on the range $\beta_3 \in [1/4, \tau^\ast].$ Looking at the slopes of $R_{\beta}(t)$ in~\eqref{eq:Rbtaulowmid} and~\eqref{eq:Rbtauupmid}, we see that the left-hand side of~\eqref{eq:function-T} is minimal when $t = r(\beta_3)$ with
\begin{align}\label{eq:return-slope2/5}
 r(\beta) = 
 \begin{cases}
   \tau^\ast -2\beta/5, \qquad &\text{ if } \beta \leqslant 5\tau^\ast/6;\\
 	3\tau^\ast/2 -\beta, &\text{ if } 5\tau^\ast/6 \leqslant \beta \leqslant \tau^\ast,
 \end{cases}	
\end{align}
and
\[
  R_{\beta_3}(r(\beta_3))-\frac{r(\beta_3)}{4} = \frac{r(\beta_3)-\tau^\ast+\beta_3}{2}-\frac{r(\beta_3)}{4} = \frac{r(\beta_3)-2\tau^\ast+2\beta_3}{4}.
  \]
Now, for $\beta_3 \in [5\tau^\ast/6, \tau^\ast]$, we obtain
\[
  R_{\beta_3}(r(\beta_3))-\frac{r(\beta_3)}{4} = \frac{\beta_3 -\tau^\ast/2}{4} \geqslant \frac{\tau^\ast}{12} > \varepsilon^{10}.
\]
and for $\beta_3 \in [1/4, 5\tau^\ast/6]$, we obtain
\[
R_{\beta_3}(r(\beta_3))-\frac{r(\beta_3)}{4} =\frac{-\tau^* +8\beta_3/5}{4} \geqslant \frac{\varepsilon}{4} >\varepsilon^{10},
\]
which completes the proof.
